papers.title: Who Observes Whom: Network Rationalizability and Its Complexity
papers.abstract: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone. When visibility is partial and asymmetric, we study the solution concepts induced by a directed \emph{observation network} $G$ in which an edge $i\to j$ means that $i$ observes $j$'s strategy. A set of profiles is \emph{self-sustaining} if every profile in it can be justified, for every player, by conjectures from the same set that agree with everything the player observes. We consider \emph{point} conjectures (single profiles) and \emph{belief} conjectures (distributions over profiles). Both range from Nash equilibrium on the complete network to point- and correlated rationalizability on the empty network, and shrink monotonically as links are added. Network topology governs both behavior and complexity. A predicted profile can be found in polynomial time on the empty network, whereas a single link makes search $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hard: under one-sided two-player monitoring, the observed player's strategies are exactly her Nash equilibrium strategies. On hierarchical networks (transitive tournaments), membership reduces recursively to smaller games and admits polynomial-size certificates, placing verification in $\exists\mathbb{R}$, and in $\mathsf{P}$ for two players. On the directed three-cycle, however, iterated elimination may never terminate under either variant, and under point conjectures interior predictions may admit only infinite witness sets, a pathology that belief conjectures avoid in the same game. Finally, when only realized pure actions are observed, the solution set is guaranteed to be non-empty exactly when the network has no edges, and is computable in time $O(n|A|^2)$.

papers.title: Paying Creators for Training Data Can Increase AI Displacement
papers.abstract: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.

papers.title: Robust Trust
papers.abstract: An agent chooses an action based on her private information and a recommendation from an informed but potentially misaligned adviser. With a known probability, the adviser truthfully reports his signal; with the remaining probability, he can send any message. We characterize robustly optimal decision rules that maximize the agent's worst-case expected payoff. Every optimal rule is equivalent to a trust-region policy in belief space: the adviser's reported beliefs are taken at face value if they fall within the trust region but are otherwise projected onto the trust region's boundary. We derive alignment thresholds above which advice is strictly valuable, explicitly characterize the solution in binary-state environments, and develop a procedure for computing the trust region numerically.

papers.title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity
papers.abstract: A network in which every bank pays in full can nevertheless admit a self-fulfilling settlement freeze under the same balance-sheet fundamentals. Thus, observing full repayment does not establish the uniqueness or robustness of the payment equilibrium. We derive this result from a precautionary-liquidity choice: banks may delay otherwise feasible payments to insure an interim funding need, trading a positive settlement-discipline cost against the marginal value of retained cash. The optimal reserve is a critical quantile of future liquidity requirements, and the repayment rule nests Eisenberg-Noe maximal feasible clearing exactly. Counterparty underpayment both reduces current cash and raises desired reserves. We characterise network amplification and the conditions for coexistence, including a homogeneous two-bank GPD frontier in which interbank exposure and maximum funding pass-through enter through one dimensionless index. A two-date settlement accounting rule distinguishes payment timing from ultimate default. The main result concerns equilibrium coexistence; the conditional best-response adjustment diagnostic does not assign selection probabilities.

papers.title: Finding pure Nash equilibria in large random games
papers.abstract: Best Response Dynamics (BRD) constitute a family of strategy update rules designed to identify Pure Nash Equilibria (PNEs) in strategic games. In each iteration, a player is selected uniformly at random and adopts a best response strategy, maximising their payoff given the current strategies of the other players. If no improvement is possible for the selected player, another is chosen. The process terminates upon reaching a state where no player wishes to deviate, corresponding to a PNE. However, convergence is not guaranteed as either PNEs may not exist, or the dynamics may become confined within substructures of the game, which we call traps, that admit no PNEs. We investigate this behaviour in the context of random games with $N$ players, each choosing between two actions and receiving independently and identically distributed payoffs. The payoff distribution is permitted to have atoms, allowing for the possibility of ties. The induced dynamics define a class of random walks on the $N$-dimensional hypercube, where the landscape includes two types of absorbing sets: PNEs and traps. Our analysis encompasses BRD, simple random walks, and a broad class of nearest-neighbour processes. We prove that, with high probability, these dynamics reach a PNE before encountering any trap. Our results complete and generalise the ones by Amiet, Collevecchio, Scarsini and Zhong (2021), using a different approach.

papers.title: TTC Domains
papers.abstract: The Top Trading Cycles (TTC) rule is fundamental to object reallocation: it is the only rule that is individually rational, pair efficient, and strategyproof on the unrestricted domain. Despite its desirable properties, at some profiles, TTC precludes longer trading cycles that could lead to more appealing allocations. We explore restricted preference domains as an avenue for finding alternative rules satisfying the three axioms. Our main contribution is to introduce a richness condition on domains, the top-two condition, and show that it characterizes TTC domains: domains to which the above characterization of TTC extends. The condition requires that, within every subset of objects, any two objects that can each be ranked first can also be ranked as the top two, in both possible orders. For every domain that fails the top-two condition, we construct a rule distinct from TTC that is individually rational, Pareto efficient, and strategyproof, and that executes longer trading cycles that TTC precludes.

papers.title: A choice-based axiomatization of Nash equilibrium
papers.abstract: An axiomatization of Nash equilibrium is provided for games of complete information in normal form. The Nash equilibrium correspondence is shown to be the unique solution concept that satisfies four simple and intuitive axioms. Two axioms reflect a mild form of individual rationality: one states that any profile of dominant strategies in a game must be a solution, whereas the other says that any solution to a game should not depend on strictly dominated strategies. The remaining two axioms are adaptations to non-cooperative games of standard choice-theoretic axioms about contraction and expansion consistency.

papers.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

papers.title: Aggregating Rankings of Coalitions to Rank Individuals
papers.abstract: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals. From university ratings to the assessment of team-sports players, we often evaluate individuals based on their coalitional performances. Although such evaluation has been addressed by cooperative game theory, it is only recently that its ordinal counterpart, social ranking theory (Moretti, 2015), has emerged. As most of the literature considers a single coalitional ranking (which corresponds to a real-valued characteristic function), we extend the model to allow a profile of coalitional rankings (which corresponds to a multidimensional characteristic function). We tackle the aggregation problem by introducing three families of inter-profile axioms, each representing how the rankings should interact or contribute to the output. After revealing fundamental impossibilities concerning the reconciliation of different families, we characterize a new solution, Pareto-extension Lex-cel (PEL), via some weaker versions of the inter-profile axioms. PEL extends Lex-cel, which is a central solution in social ranking theory, by analogy with Sen's Pareto extension rule. Our results develop the connection between classical Arrovian aggregation, cooperative game theory, and social ranking theory.

papers.title: Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations
papers.abstract: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

papers.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
papers.abstract: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

papers.title: Knowing Less After a Diagnostic Test: Dilation in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Dilation (Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993) occurs when conditioning on new information \textit{only} increases uncertainty regardless of what the information reveals. Often viewed as an undesirable feature of models of ambiguity, dilation has sparked sustained debate about belief updating. This paper shows that following established clinical guidance can induce dilation, even for diagnostic tests that meet conventional performance benchmarks. We characterize when a test is dilation-inducing and show that a ubiquitous feature of performance studies -- evaluating tests against an imperfect reference -- creates scope for dilation. To facilitate detection before clinical use and inform regulatory standards, we develop a finite-sample valid hypothesis test of the null that a diagnostic test is dilation-inducing in this context. Applying the method to an influential study that preceded and contributed to the clinical adoption of chest CT screening for COVID-19, we find that the data are consistent with dilation.

papers.title: When Better Artificial Intelligence Widens the Adoption Gap in Health Care
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist healthcare providers in clinical practice or replace services for which they are paid. We model how provider influence shapes two policy choices. The first is adoption, the share of cases in which coverage is switched to care using AI. The second is the review requirement, the number of paid reviews that must accompany AI when it is used in clinical care. Assistance can lower providers' costs and increase their profits while leaving paid reviews unaffected. However, increasingly capable AI may support autonomous use that can replace reviews and reduce providers' profits. Provider gains from adoption first rise and subsequently fall as AI capability improves. Hence, providers oppose sufficiently autonomous AI if their lost income from reviews exceeds savings from better assistance. Opposition to AI adoption arises earlier for AI that displaces more reviews. When providers can influence adoption but not the review requirement, their opposition causes under-adoption. The patient value forgone at the margin grows as AI improves. At interior policies, provider influence over both decisions widens adoption and raises review requirements above the patient optimum.

papers.title: Pricing Expertise with Information Spillovers
papers.abstract: Why do experts charge value-based fees for some services and flat fees for others? For example, an analyst charges the same fee for a stock report whether the client invests a thousand dollars or a million, while an investment bank charges a higher fee for a fairness opinion on a large merger than on a small one. We consider the problem of an expert who sells expertise to a client whose private type determines his project and how much he has at stake. Because project states are correlated, cheaper expertise about a related project can substitute for expertise about his own. We develop a Markov model of information spillovers and provide an explicit characterization of the optimal menu. With perfect spillovers, as with a stock report, a common flat fee for full information is optimal. With sufficiently weak spillovers, as with a fairness opinion, each client receives full information at a value-based fee equal to his willingness to pay. Between these extremes, low types can receive distorted expertise at their full willingness to pay, while middle and high types receive full information. Middle types pay a common base fee plus a project-specific fee that rises with what is at stake, and high types pay a value-based fee equal to their willingness to pay. Because higher types lose more by buying expertise about another project, the project-specific fee can rise faster than willingness to pay, so client surplus can peak among middle types and fall to zero at the top.

papers.title: Affirmative Action in India with Hierarchical Reservations
papers.abstract: We study the design of affirmative action mechanisms, focusing on India's system of horizontal reservations within vertical reservations. We consider a one-to-all policy, under which an applicant eligible for multiple horizontal categories simultaneously contributes toward each category's minimum guarantee. When horizontal reservations have a hierarchical structure, we introduce a choice rule that selects the unique merit-optimal set of applicants subject to these guaranties, satisfies the substitutes condition and size monotonicity. In a matching-with-contracts framework, we show that the generalized deferred acceptance mechanism is stable, strategy-proof, and eliminates justified envy under aggregate choice rules using the hierarchical choice rule in each vertical category. We establish a fundamental trade-off between merit and affirmative action between the one-to-all and one-to-one counting policies.

papers.title: Hidden Eligibility and the Credibility of Adoption
papers.abstract: Subsidies encourage adoption, but they also change what others can learn from it. We study a government that chooses the amount and coverage of an early-adoption rebate and the information released about eligibility. Both early and late adoption create positive externalities. When eligibility is hidden, expanding the programme makes adoption less informative. As the benefit of early adoption rises, the optimal programme jumps from a small one that preserves imitation to a larger one that gives it up. We show that partial disclosure can support intermediate coverage and strictly improve on both optimally chosen opacity and full disclosure. An optimal report certifies the eligibility of some users, leaving the remaining adoptions sufficiently persuasive to induce imitation. We characterise the conditions for this policy and compare coverage under the alternative reporting rules. Analytical extensions allow delivery failures, private information, and heterogeneous adoption costs. The discontinuous change in optimal coverage can persist even when cost heterogeneity makes welfare continuous in coverage.

papers.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
papers.abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. We identify two reversal phenomena in the optimal mechanism. First, the principal's expected payoff is strictly higher in the first period than in the second, even though she is better informed after the review. Second, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but less funding following a bad review, and may receive less funding following a good review as well.

papers.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design: Joint Optimization of Contracting, Information-Production Technology, and Disclosure
papers.abstract: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly optimizes contracting, information-production technology, and disclosure across a broad class of economic environments with general allocation constraints. Hidden actions, endogenous information acquisition, learning, and disclosure interact through dynamic incentives. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish the Dynamic Revelation Principle, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Under private values with informational interdependence, we characterize joint incentives through choice obedience, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, and global integral monotonicity. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, dynamic revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions of either sign and branched outcomes. Applications show Milgrom-Weber revenue-ranking reversal with endogenous acquisition, no efficient first-price equilibrium under Gaussian signals, and absent, interior, or full financial-contract disclosure.
